lessons.title: Liquidity, Management Effort and Exit Options

children.text: Suresh needs ₹60 lakh in three months for his daughter's master's degree abroad. On paper he is comfortably rich: a ₹1.2 crore flat in Kochi and a ₹1.5 crore pre-leased shop nearby. But he cannot sell half a flat. His shop tenant's lock-in ends in eight months, which worries buyers. And a quick sale of either means accepting whatever price the first serious buyer offers. Meanwhile, a colleague with ₹60 lakh in mutual funds redeems on Zerodha Coin and has the money in a few working days. Returns on paper mean little if you cannot get the money out when life demands it.

body.text: A home sells best empty, to a family that wants to live in it. A commercial property sells best leased, to an investor who wants its rent. Plan the exit before you buy, because you cannot fix it when you are in a hurry.

children.text: Liquidity: Who Will Buy From You?

Liquidity in property comes down to how many buyers exist and how easily they can pay. Residential property has the biggest buyer pool in Indian real estate: families buying to live in, investors buying to rent, and NRIs buying for later. Most of them can get a home loan, which makes the pool even deeper.

Commercial property has a narrower pool: HNIs and family offices seeking yield, businesses buying their own premises, and, for large Grade A assets, institutional funds and REITs. Bank finance for these buyers is costlier and harder to get. A vacant commercial unit is the least liquid of all, because it appeals to neither yield investors nor most businesses until someone commits to occupying it.

markDefs.definition: A firm or individual that handles tenant search, agreements, rent collection, repairs and move-outs on an owner's behalf, for a fee usually linked to the rent.

children.text: Owners who do not want the effort can hire a

. Fees are usually tied to rent, and on a residential yield of 2% to 3%, even a modest fee takes a noticeable share of your income. Commercial owners more often rely on brokers at leasing time and lawyers for documents, with less day-to-day management.

body.text: Effort has a cost even if you never pay for it. If you spend 40 hours a year managing a flat that yields ₹3 lakh net, you are working for about ₹7,500 an hour. Worth it for some people, not for others. Count your time before you call rental income passive.

children.text: Exit Options and How to Time Them

body.title: Getting the best price on exit

columns.label: Residential: sell vacant
points: End users pay the most, and they want to move in
A tenanted flat narrows buyers to investors, who pay less
Time the sale to the end of an 11-month agreement
Freshly painted, empty homes photograph and show better
Bank loans for buyers are straightforward on ready flats

columns.label: Commercial: sell leased
points: Yield investors pay for secure income
A long remaining lock-in lowers the cap rate buyers demand
Sell after a renewal or fresh lease, not near lock-in expiry
A vacant unit is valued on hope, not income
Owner-occupier businesses are the exception, and they are few

body.title: Planning the sale of a leased office unit

events.title: Review the lease
events.description: Check remaining lock-in, next escalation and renewal terms. Buyers pay most when several years of lock-in remain.

events.title: Talk to the tenant
events.description: If lock-in is short, negotiate an extension or fresh lease, even with a small concession on rent.

events.title: Clean up paperwork
events.description: Gather lease deed, occupancy certificate, tax receipts, CAM clearance, GST and TDS records.

events.title: Get a valuation and appoint brokers
events.description: Test the market with yield investors; set a price based on net income and realistic cap rates.

events.title: Negotiate and sign
events.description: Agree price, deposit transfer and closing date; plan capital gains tax or reinvestment.

events.title: Register and hand over
events.description: Execute sale deed, collect sale proceeds net of the buyer's TDS, and obtain the tenant's attornment letter.

markDefs.definition: A secured loan where an existing property is mortgaged to raise money for other needs. Banks typically lend a portion of the property's market value, lower for commercial than for residential property.

children.text: Sometimes the smartest exit is not selling at all. A
lets you borrow against a flat or commercial unit you already own, usually at a lower rate than personal loans, while keeping the asset and its future appreciation or rent.

body.title: When a loan against property beats a quick sale

children.text: A LAP makes sense when the cash need is temporary, when a forced sale would mean a large liquidity discount, or when selling would trigger capital gains tax you would rather avoid. It is a poor choice when the underlying problem is that you cannot afford the property, because it adds an EMI on top.

Lenders usually offer a lower share of value, and sometimes a higher rate, against commercial property than residential. For a leased commercial unit, lease rental discounting may raise more money at a better rate, because the loan is backed by the tenant's rent.

body.text: Listed REITs trade on NSE and BSE like shares, which solves the liquidity problem for commercial exposure. Fractional ownership and SM REIT platforms are different: many have limited or no active secondary market, so exiting before the platform sells the asset can be slow. Check the exit mechanism before you invest, not after.

body.title: Calculate: The Cost of Selling in a Hurry
body.prompt: A commercial unit in Indore would fetch ₹2.4 crore with a patient sale. You need cash urgently and accept a price 15% below that, then pay 2% brokerage on the sale price. How much do you receive before tax, in ₹ lakh? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Sale price: ₹2.4 crore × 0.85 = ₹2.04 crore. After 2% brokerage: ₹2.04 crore × 0.98 = ₹1.9992 crore, about ₹199.9 lakh. A patient sale at ₹2.4 crore less the same 2% brokerage would have given ₹2.352 crore, so rushing cost about ₹35.3 lakh.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Unit Sells Best?
body.question: You own four similar office units in the same Hyderabad building. Which is likely to sell fastest and at the best price to an investor?
options: The unit that has been vacant for a year
The unit leased to a listed company with 6 years of lock-in remaining
The unit leased to a startup whose lock-in ends in 3 months
The unit you have just repainted but not leased
body.explanation: Investors buy commercial property for secure income. A strong tenant with 6 years of lock-in gives them exactly that, so they accept a lower cap rate and pay more. Vacant or soon-to-expire units are priced on uncertainty.

body.title: Scenario: An NRI Exiting Kochi
body.scenario: Thomas, an NRI working in Dubai, owns a 3BHK flat in Kochi rented to a family on an 11-month agreement that ends in 5 months, and a pre-leased shop leased to a national pharmacy chain whose lock-in ends in 14 months. He wants to exit both within a year to buy a home in Dubai, and he rarely visits India.
body.prompt: How should Thomas sequence and prepare the two sales?
body.modelAnswer: Sell the flat first, vacant. He should not renew the family's agreement, give notice as the agreement requires, repaint, and list it as soon as it is empty, because families pay the best prices for ready, vacant homes. For the shop, the short remaining lock-in is his biggest problem. He should approach the pharmacy chain now about extending the lease or signing a fresh lock-in, even with a small rent concession, and sell only once that is done, since a 5-year lock-in could lift the price far more than the concession costs. Practically, he should appoint a trusted person with a registered power of attorney to handle viewings and registration, gather documents early, and speak to a CA about tax. As an NRI seller, buyers must deduct TDS at a much higher rate than for resident sellers, so he may want to apply for a lower TDS certificate and plan how the proceeds will be repatriated.

body.title: Plan Your Exit Before You Buy
steps: Ask who the likely buyers will be in 5 to 10 years, and whether banks will lend to them
For flats, prefer locations and layouts that appeal to end users, not only investors
For commercial units, prefer strong tenants and buildings where leases can be renewed easily
Avoid assets whose only exit is a single type of buyer
Keep a cash buffer so you are never forced to sell in a hurry
Know how you could raise cash without selling, such as a loan against property or LRD
For fractional or SM REIT investments, confirm how and when you can exit

The range of people and institutions willing and able to buy an asset.

points: Residential property has the largest buyer pool, but even a good flat takes months to sell and cannot be sold in parts.
Commercial property has fewer buyers; leased units sell to yield investors, while vacant units are the hardest to exit.
Homes usually fetch the best price vacant; commercial units fetch the best price with a strong tenant and a long lock-in.
Residential ownership means frequent small tasks; commercial ownership means rare but high-stakes ones.
Selling in a hurry can cost a large liquidity discount, so keep a cash buffer and plan exits years ahead.
A loan against property or LRD can raise cash without selling, and listed REITs offer commercial exposure with daily liquidity.

body.text: Selling times, brokerage, discounts and fee levels in this lesson are indicative and vary by city, asset and market conditions. Loan terms and tax rules, especially for NRIs, should be confirmed with lenders and a qualified tax professional. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any property.
